medical.title: Targeted antibody treatment reverses diabetic nerve damage in mouse models
medical.summary: A team of UTHealth Houston researchers slowed and even reversed diabetic nerve damage in mice, bringing researchers one step closer to developing a treatment for humans. The research is published in Science Translational Medicine.

medical.title: Blood protein analysis could help diagnose rare diseases missed by genome sequencing
medical.summary: Researchers from Queen Mary University of London, the Berlin Institute of Health at Charité (BIH) and Genomics England have shown that measuring proteins in the blood can provide important additional clues about the effects of genetic variants, helping to identify diagnoses and potential new disease-causing genes that genome sequencing alone has been unable to resolve.

medical.title: Personalized home-visiting support may reduce postnatal depression among young first-time mothers
medical.summary: The Early Partnership program combined sustained relationship-based support, practical assistance and coordinated multidisciplinary care from pregnancy until 12 months after childbirth. Compared with young mothers receiving standard publicly funded maternal and child health services, participants in the program reported improvements that were maintained at both six and 12 months after childbirth.

medical.title: Nasal spray vaccine protects against bird flu in mice
medical.summary: WashU Medicine researchers led by Jacco Boon, a professor in the John T. Milliken Department of Medicine, report that an experimental bird flu vaccine provides strong immune protection in mice, including in animals previously vaccinated against seasonal flu. Because pre-existing immunity from prior seasonal influenza infection or vaccination could diminish the efficacy of H5N1 vaccines, showing that the new vaccine succeeds alongside existing immunity is a crucial milestone.

medical.title: Current blood pressure thresholds may miss critically injured children
medical.summary: Blood pressure thresholds commonly used to identify dangerously unstable vital signs in children may not signal trouble soon enough after a traumatic injury, according to a national study of more than 230,000 pediatric trauma patients. The findings suggest clinicians may need to recognize and respond to signs of circulatory instability at higher blood pressure levels than current pediatric reference values indicate.

medical.title: Blood test could monitor bone metastasis in medullary thyroid cancer
medical.summary: Researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center have uncovered a possible reason why metastatic medullary thyroid cancer causes abnormal bone growth, pointing to a new opportunity to detect and monitor bone metastases in patients.

medical.title: We designed a new way to build miniature fluidic devices to enable personalized cancer treatment
medical.summary: There is no "one-size-fits-all" treatment for patients living with cancer. Cancer occurs when normal cells in the body genetically mutate and transform into abnormal cells that divide uncontrollably.

medical.title: Inhibitor may turn tumor-protecting immune cells against glioblastoma
medical.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers have identified a potential new approach to treating glioblastoma that could help the immune system fight the aggressive brain cancer while improving the effectiveness of existing chemotherapy.

medical.title: Does debriefing about a difficult birth stop it turning into trauma?
medical.summary: For some women, the birth of their baby is one of the happiest days of their lives. Others remember it as a frightening, overwhelming or deeply distressing experience. About 1 in 3 women report their birth experience as traumatic.

medical.title: The weight‑loss drug divide: Private prescribing is lowest where need is greatest
medical.summary: For many people living with obesity, Wegovy and Mounjaro offer the possibility of substantial weight loss without surgery. Yet data from one private provider points to a troubling divide: Prescription rates of these drugs in England are lowest in communities where obesity is most common.

medical.title: Women who hit menopause early see faster brain aging and earlier Alzheimer's diagnosis
medical.summary: Menopause is more than just the end of a woman's reproductive years. It brings a cascade of hormonal changes that can affect overall well-being, giving rise to a range of physical and emotional symptoms. A recent study published in JAMA Network Open has found that a woman's age at menopause is connected to her long-term neurological health and brain structure.

medical.title: Early signs of eczema, food allergies may appear on infants' skin
medical.summary: The first clues that a baby may develop eczema or food allergies could be hiding in the microscopic organisms living on their skin, according to a study led by researchers in Washington State University's College of Veterinary Medicine.

medical.title: Cognitive behavioral therapy may reduce biological aging among older adults with insomnia
medical.summary: In a new study published in The Lancet Healthy Longevity, UCLA Health researchers found that older adults who underwent cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia were more likely to experience insomnia remission and a slower pace of biological aging than a control group that received sleep education.

medical.title: Q&A: Discovery could lead to a cure for glaucoma with nanotherapy
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of Virginia and Northwestern University have created a tool that could help cure glaucoma.

medical.title: Removing cGAS protein may make aging worse by unleashing inflammatory DNA
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of Rochester thought that shutting down a protein linked to inflammation might help slow aging. Instead, they found the opposite: Without the protein, mice became frailer, experienced more inflammation and had shorter life spans.

medical.title: Anemia in pregnancy linked to differences in babies' brain development
medical.summary: Researchers using a portable MRI scanner found that measurable differences in brain volumes emerged at around 12 months of age, offering some of the earliest evidence yet that maternal anemia shapes infant brain development in the first year of life and beyond.

medical.title: Women with cerebral palsy miss vital gynecologic care, study finds
medical.summary: As more individuals with cerebral palsy live well into adulthood, medical professionals are taking a closer look at the unique long-term health care needs of this patient population. While adults with cerebral palsy require the same routine health maintenance as anyone else, a large national study conducted at Yale showed that women living with cerebral palsy received significantly less preventive gynecologic care than women without the condition.

medical.title: Improved health should guide obesity treatment, not weight loss alone
medical.summary: A new scientific statement released today by the Endocrine Society highlights the benefits of obesity treatment beyond weight loss, including improved overall health and reduced risk of conditions such as heart disease, sleep apnea and liver disease.

medical.title: Clinical trial supports adding mental health care to routine preparation for major surgery
medical.summary: Facing major surgery is stressful, but for older adults, unaddressed anxiety and depression can impede physical recovery. A clinical trial led by researchers at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis found that starting an intervention before surgery—one that combines mental health coaching with optimization of medications that may increase risks for older adults—reduces postsurgery anxiety and depression.

medical.title: Stanford scientists discover a seafood that can reverse signs of aging
medical.summary: A substance found in edible sea squirts appeared to reverse several signs of aging in older mice. Plasmalogen supplements improved memory and learning, strengthened connections between brain cells, reduced inflammation, and even helped the mice grow thicker, darker hair. Researchers believe the compounds may encourage brain regeneration and protect aging synapses.

medical.title: Scientists reveal the hidden instructions that build the human brain
medical.summary: UCLA researchers have discovered two powerful influences that help guide how the human brain forms before birth. Radial glia, stem cells responsible for producing much of the cerebral cortex, change their behavior depending on how they process glucose and on physical contact with signals arriving from the thalamus. Those signals can alter which types of neurons are produced, including upper-layer neurons that are especially prominent in humans.

medical.title: New injectable treatment helps the brain rebuild after stroke
medical.summary: Duke researchers developed an injectable scaffold that helped stroke-damaged brains grow new blood vessels, support nerve regrowth, and recover movement in mice. The treatment appears to work partly by recruiting the body’s own immune cells, including neutrophils that may switch from damaging to helpful under the right conditions.

science.title: Body-related TikTok content linked to self-objectification and mood
science.summary: Viewing "thinspiration" content on TikTok increases self-objectification and worsens mood, while viewing body-positive content also increases self-objectification but is linked to a more positive mood, according to a new study published in PLOS One by Samantha Jones of Western University, Canada, and colleagues.

science.title: 'Here, There and Everywhere': The Beatles have permeated research papers across academic disciplines
science.summary: More than 3,000 scientific article titles across disciplines have made use of Beatles song titles and lyrics, according to a study published in PLOS One by Gabriel Budel of Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands and colleagues. This analysis is an unprecedentedly large-scale, cross-disciplinary account of how the Beatles have left their mark on scientific writing.

science.title: Fossils from embryo to adult suggest how an enigmatic, bird-like troodontid dinosaur grew
science.summary: Analysis of fossilized remains from dinosaurs known as troodontids reveals how one species' hip and leg bones may have developed over its lifespan, from embryo to adult—with potential implications for resolving longstanding taxonomic challenges. David Varricchio of Montana State University, U.S., and Heath Caldwell of North Carolina State University, U.S., present their findings in the journal PLOS One on Sept. 9, 2026.

science.title: Asian elephants can resist impulsive behavior, researchers find
science.summary: Researchers at the CUNY Graduate Center and Hunter College have found that Asian elephants can suppress impulsive behaviors and adjust their actions when circumstances change—a cognitive ability that may help explain the animals' sophisticated problem-solving skills and social behavior.

science.title: JWST discovers that Chariklo's invisible rings are changing
science.summary: Until just over a decade ago, ring systems were thought to be exclusive to the giant planets of the solar system, such as Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. However, in 2013, a small body barely 250 kilometers (155 miles) in diameter, located at nearly 17 times the Earth–sun distance, joined this small group. The object is Chariklo, a small body orbiting between Saturn and Uranus, around which astronomers discovered two dense rings.

science.title: Ice Age origins of one of humanity's oldest drug habits discovered
science.summary: A team of Griffith University archaeologists has uncovered evidence that humans were using mind-altering substances much earlier than previously supposed.

science.title: Decades-old DNA mystery solved after strands are captured zipping together for the first time
science.summary: Researchers have captured the moment two DNA molecules zip together, overcoming their identical negative charges to pair up and revealing a mechanism that has puzzled scientists for more than 20 years. Using high-powered atomic force microscopy, scientists at the University of Sheffield and the University of York directly imaged two DNA double helices locking together, marking the first time this fundamental biological process has been visualized.

science.title: Liquid gold: Could we turn our urine into fertilizer?
science.summary: For thousands of years, human urine has had real value. After our bodies absorb nutrients from our food, they excrete the rest—mainly via urine. An adult produces about 500 liters (132 gallons) a year. This liquid gold is very rich in nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, three nutrients vital for plant growth.

science.title: The Anthropocene was rejected as a geological epoch—but the idea is still changing how we see the world
science.summary: The Anthropocene became part of the zeitgeist after Nobel laureate Paul Crutzen launched the idea in 2000. This is the notion that a crescendo of human impacts has recently propelled Earth out of the relatively stable climatic conditions of the Holocene epoch, during which human civilization developed and flourished, to produce a new kind of planet.

science.title: Canada's last epishelf lake is gone for good, study confirms
science.summary: Canada's last epishelf lake drained into the Arctic Ocean following the 2020 breakup of the Milne Ice Shelf and will not recover, a new study confirms.

science.title: When benefit corporations get certified, is it 'greenwashing' in stereo?
science.summary: The term "benefit corporation" is becoming increasingly familiar as a label for companies with a hybrid commitment to the social good and profit-making. Interestingly, the term itself has taken on a hybrid meaning.

science.title: Restoring Australia's she-oaks means listening to Indigenous knowledges
science.summary: In Australia, many Indigenous communities have connections and stories linked to the she-oak.

science.title: Tiny 2D cracks creep through materials before triggering sudden fracture, experiments reveal
science.summary: We have all seen something suddenly break: a phone screen cracks, a plastic object snaps or a piece of glass shatters. To our eyes, the failure seems to happen all at once. But what if the most important part of the break happens long before the final snap?

science.title: The 'costly son' hypothesis: Why bigger sons may make births riskier across species
science.summary: A new comparative review, published in The Anatomical Record, examines factors that may lead to birth complications among humans and other mammals. The study suggests that fetal sex may play an important role in risky births in humans and several other species.

science.title: Taking the sting out of fire ants with genomics
science.summary: Fire ants have earned their reputation as one of Australia's most damaging invasive pests. From ruined picnics to serious impacts on agriculture, biodiversity and public health, they are notoriously difficult to control.

science.title: Layer-based design offers new route to topological magnets
science.summary: Topological quantum materials combine unusual electronic states with properties such as magnetism or superconductivity, offering possibilities for future electronics and quantum technologies. Researchers at Tohoku University have now shown that changing the number of layers in a crystal can provide a systematic way to design topological magnets. The work is published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society.

science.title: Forever chemicals break apart into fluoride under UV treatment, revealing a cleanup roadmap
science.summary: UC Riverside environmental engineers have identified key chemical reactions that occur when ultraviolet light is used to destroy "forever chemical" pollutants in water, providing a roadmap for developing more effective cleanup technologies.

science.title: UK subsidies for land-based seafood farming would boost tree-planting policy
science.summary: Subsidies for emerging technology that allows seafood to be produced on land would boost the UK's food security and deliver significant climate benefits, new research shows.

science.title: How we manage and engage with horses may shape their personality
science.summary: A new study reveals that horse personality is not only a matter of genetics, age or breed but also systematically linked to how horses are housed, ridden and cared for, and to the quality of the relationship they share with their owners. The findings underscore the importance of everyday management decisions for equine personality and welfare.

science.title: The Future We Choose: New Beyond Blue report explores the forces shaping the next decade of mental health in Australia
science.summary: Beyond Blue has launched "The Future We Choose: Mental health support in Australia through the next decade of change," a new strategic foresight report by Australia's national science agency, CSIRO, exploring how mental health in Australia may evolve over the next decade and the choices that could help shape a stronger, more connected and resilient future.

science.title: New AI model for DNA learns from evolution to unlock secrets of the human genome
science.summary: More than two decades after scientists first sequenced the entire human genome—all 3 billion base pairs, of DNA code—the meaning of much of this code remains a mystery.

science.title: Petrochemical industry emissions could climb 50% by 2050, global mapping suggests
science.summary: Carbon emissions from the petrochemical industry could increase by 50% by 2050, according to new research from the University of Sheffield. The study, published in Nature Sustainability, provides the most detailed data to date on emissions from one of the world's biggest emitters of carbon dioxide.

science.title: White is more than a color: How nature inspired a new sustainable way to make white, water-repellent materials
science.summary: Look closely at Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa, one of Japan's most iconic masterpieces. The brilliant white of the waves, snow on Mount Fuji and clouds above contain no white pigment. Instead, their whiteness comes from the way light scatters off the unprinted fibers of the washi paper itself.

science.title: First Denisovan forearm bone discovered in southwest China
science.summary: Scientists have discovered various Denisovan remains in Southwest China dating to the late Middle Pleistocene, including the first Denisovan radius—one of two long bones in the forearm.

science.title: A 'wholistic' view of cellular communication across an entire animal
science.summary: It can't be heard, but different parts of the human body are in constant conversation, communicating to keep the entire system running efficiently. For biologists, being able to listen in on this discussion is a long-sought-after goal. Over the years, researchers have caught snippets of these exchanges, but the complete dialogue has remained out of reach.

environment.title: Marine conservation collides with mining in Indonesia’s biodiversity-rich Moramo Bay
environment.summary: SOUTH KONAWE, Indonesia — A marine protected area in Indonesia’s Southeast Sulawesi province is home to a critically depleted population of humphead wrasse. The species presence helped the area gain its protected status, but mining permits overlap parts of the conservation zone and line its coast. environment.title: Galaxy Gallery: Galactic Gems Glisten in New Gallery From NASA’s Chandra
environment.summary: This gallery displays a collection of 16 galactic images from Chandra and other telescopes. Astronomers put galaxies into three main categories: spirals like our own Milky Way, ellipticals that are older and likely the results of mergers, and irregulars that can encompass a wide range of galactic phenomena. All types are represented in this collection. Each galactic image contains X-ray data from Chandra combined with data from telescopes such as NASA’s Webb, Hubble, IXPE, Swift, and NuSTAR, and others both in space and on the ground. The post Galaxy Gallery: Galactic Gems Glisten in New Gallery From NASA’s Chandra appeared first on NASA Science .

environment.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
environment.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

environment.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
environment.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

environment.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
environment.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

environment.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
environment.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.

mix_items.title: Body-related TikTok content linked to self-objectification and mood
mix_items.summary: Viewing "thinspiration" content on TikTok increases self-objectification and worsens mood, while viewing body-positive content also increases self-objectification but is linked to a more positive mood, according to a new study published in PLOS One by Samantha Jones of Western University, Canada, and colleagues.

mix_items.title: 'Here, There and Everywhere': The Beatles have permeated research papers across academic disciplines
mix_items.summary: More than 3,000 scientific article titles across disciplines have made use of Beatles song titles and lyrics, according to a study published in PLOS One by Gabriel Budel of Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands and colleagues. This analysis is an unprecedentedly large-scale, cross-disciplinary account of how the Beatles have left their mark on scientific writing.

mix_items.title: Fossils from embryo to adult suggest how an enigmatic, bird-like troodontid dinosaur grew
mix_items.summary: Analysis of fossilized remains from dinosaurs known as troodontids reveals how one species' hip and leg bones may have developed over its lifespan, from embryo to adult—with potential implications for resolving longstanding taxonomic challenges. David Varricchio of Montana State University, U.S., and Heath Caldwell of North Carolina State University, U.S., present their findings in the journal PLOS One on Sept. 9, 2026.

mix_items.title: Targeted antibody treatment reverses diabetic nerve damage in mouse models
mix_items.summary: A team of UTHealth Houston researchers slowed and even reversed diabetic nerve damage in mice, bringing researchers one step closer to developing a treatment for humans. The research is published in Science Translational Medicine.

mix_items.title: Asian elephants can resist impulsive behavior, researchers find
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the CUNY Graduate Center and Hunter College have found that Asian elephants can suppress impulsive behaviors and adjust their actions when circumstances change—a cognitive ability that may help explain the animals' sophisticated problem-solving skills and social behavior.

mix_items.title: Blood protein analysis could help diagnose rare diseases missed by genome sequencing
mix_items.summary: Researchers from Queen Mary University of London, the Berlin Institute of Health at Charité (BIH) and Genomics England have shown that measuring proteins in the blood can provide important additional clues about the effects of genetic variants, helping to identify diagnoses and potential new disease-causing genes that genome sequencing alone has been unable to resolve.

mix_items.title: JWST discovers that Chariklo's invisible rings are changing
mix_items.summary: Until just over a decade ago, ring systems were thought to be exclusive to the giant planets of the solar system, such as Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. However, in 2013, a small body barely 250 kilometers (155 miles) in diameter, located at nearly 17 times the Earth–sun distance, joined this small group. The object is Chariklo, a small body orbiting between Saturn and Uranus, around which astronomers discovered two dense rings.

mix_items.title: Ice Age origins of one of humanity's oldest drug habits discovered
mix_items.summary: A team of Griffith University archaeologists has uncovered evidence that humans were using mind-altering substances much earlier than previously supposed.

mix_items.title: Decades-old DNA mystery solved after strands are captured zipping together for the first time
mix_items.summary: Researchers have captured the moment two DNA molecules zip together, overcoming their identical negative charges to pair up and revealing a mechanism that has puzzled scientists for more than 20 years. Using high-powered atomic force microscopy, scientists at the University of Sheffield and the University of York directly imaged two DNA double helices locking together, marking the first time this fundamental biological process has been visualized.

mix_items.title: Personalized home-visiting support may reduce postnatal depression among young first-time mothers
mix_items.summary: The Early Partnership program combined sustained relationship-based support, practical assistance and coordinated multidisciplinary care from pregnancy until 12 months after childbirth. Compared with young mothers receiving standard publicly funded maternal and child health services, participants in the program reported improvements that were maintained at both six and 12 months after childbirth.

mix_items.title: Nasal spray vaccine protects against bird flu in mice
mix_items.summary: WashU Medicine researchers led by Jacco Boon, a professor in the John T. Milliken Department of Medicine, report that an experimental bird flu vaccine provides strong immune protection in mice, including in animals previously vaccinated against seasonal flu. Because pre-existing immunity from prior seasonal influenza infection or vaccination could diminish the efficacy of H5N1 vaccines, showing that the new vaccine succeeds alongside existing immunity is a crucial milestone.

mix_items.title: Liquid gold: Could we turn our urine into fertilizer?
mix_items.summary: For thousands of years, human urine has had real value. After our bodies absorb nutrients from our food, they excrete the rest—mainly via urine. An adult produces about 500 liters (132 gallons) a year. This liquid gold is very rich in nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, three nutrients vital for plant growth.

mix_items.title: Current blood pressure thresholds may miss critically injured children
mix_items.summary: Blood pressure thresholds commonly used to identify dangerously unstable vital signs in children may not signal trouble soon enough after a traumatic injury, according to a national study of more than 230,000 pediatric trauma patients. The findings suggest clinicians may need to recognize and respond to signs of circulatory instability at higher blood pressure levels than current pediatric reference values indicate.

mix_items.title: The Anthropocene was rejected as a geological epoch—but the idea is still changing how we see the world
mix_items.summary: The Anthropocene became part of the zeitgeist after Nobel laureate Paul Crutzen launched the idea in 2000. This is the notion that a crescendo of human impacts has recently propelled Earth out of the relatively stable climatic conditions of the Holocene epoch, during which human civilization developed and flourished, to produce a new kind of planet.

mix_items.title: Blood test could monitor bone metastasis in medullary thyroid cancer
mix_items.summary: Researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center have uncovered a possible reason why metastatic medullary thyroid cancer causes abnormal bone growth, pointing to a new opportunity to detect and monitor bone metastases in patients.

mix_items.title: Canada's last epishelf lake is gone for good, study confirms
mix_items.summary: Canada's last epishelf lake drained into the Arctic Ocean following the 2020 breakup of the Milne Ice Shelf and will not recover, a new study confirms.

mix_items.title: We designed a new way to build miniature fluidic devices to enable personalized cancer treatment
mix_items.summary: There is no "one-size-fits-all" treatment for patients living with cancer. Cancer occurs when normal cells in the body genetically mutate and transform into abnormal cells that divide uncontrollably.

mix_items.title: When benefit corporations get certified, is it 'greenwashing' in stereo?
mix_items.summary: The term "benefit corporation" is becoming increasingly familiar as a label for companies with a hybrid commitment to the social good and profit-making. Interestingly, the term itself has taken on a hybrid meaning.

mix_items.title: Restoring Australia's she-oaks means listening to Indigenous knowledges
mix_items.summary: In Australia, many Indigenous communities have connections and stories linked to the she-oak.

mix_items.title: Inhibitor may turn tumor-protecting immune cells against glioblastoma
mix_items.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers have identified a potential new approach to treating glioblastoma that could help the immune system fight the aggressive brain cancer while improving the effectiveness of existing chemotherapy.

mix_items.title: Does debriefing about a difficult birth stop it turning into trauma?
mix_items.summary: For some women, the birth of their baby is one of the happiest days of their lives. Others remember it as a frightening, overwhelming or deeply distressing experience. About 1 in 3 women report their birth experience as traumatic.

mix_items.title: Tiny 2D cracks creep through materials before triggering sudden fracture, experiments reveal
mix_items.summary: We have all seen something suddenly break: a phone screen cracks, a plastic object snaps or a piece of glass shatters. To our eyes, the failure seems to happen all at once. But what if the most important part of the break happens long before the final snap?

mix_items.title: The 'costly son' hypothesis: Why bigger sons may make births riskier across species
mix_items.summary: A new comparative review, published in The Anatomical Record, examines factors that may lead to birth complications among humans and other mammals. The study suggests that fetal sex may play an important role in risky births in humans and several other species.

mix_items.title: Taking the sting out of fire ants with genomics
mix_items.summary: Fire ants have earned their reputation as one of Australia's most damaging invasive pests. From ruined picnics to serious impacts on agriculture, biodiversity and public health, they are notoriously difficult to control.

mix_items.title: The weight‑loss drug divide: Private prescribing is lowest where need is greatest
mix_items.summary: For many people living with obesity, Wegovy and Mounjaro offer the possibility of substantial weight loss without surgery. Yet data from one private provider points to a troubling divide: Prescription rates of these drugs in England are lowest in communities where obesity is most common.

mix_items.title: Layer-based design offers new route to topological magnets
mix_items.summary: Topological quantum materials combine unusual electronic states with properties such as magnetism or superconductivity, offering possibilities for future electronics and quantum technologies. Researchers at Tohoku University have now shown that changing the number of layers in a crystal can provide a systematic way to design topological magnets. The work is published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society.

mix_items.title: Women who hit menopause early see faster brain aging and earlier Alzheimer's diagnosis
mix_items.summary: Menopause is more than just the end of a woman's reproductive years. It brings a cascade of hormonal changes that can affect overall well-being, giving rise to a range of physical and emotional symptoms. A recent study published in JAMA Network Open has found that a woman's age at menopause is connected to her long-term neurological health and brain structure.

mix_items.title: Early signs of eczema, food allergies may appear on infants' skin
mix_items.summary: The first clues that a baby may develop eczema or food allergies could be hiding in the microscopic organisms living on their skin, according to a study led by researchers in Washington State University's College of Veterinary Medicine.

mix_items.title: Cognitive behavioral therapy may reduce biological aging among older adults with insomnia
mix_items.summary: In a new study published in The Lancet Healthy Longevity, UCLA Health researchers found that older adults who underwent cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia were more likely to experience insomnia remission and a slower pace of biological aging than a control group that received sleep education.

mix_items.title: Forever chemicals break apart into fluoride under UV treatment, revealing a cleanup roadmap
mix_items.summary: UC Riverside environmental engineers have identified key chemical reactions that occur when ultraviolet light is used to destroy "forever chemical" pollutants in water, providing a roadmap for developing more effective cleanup technologies.

mix_items.title: UK subsidies for land-based seafood farming would boost tree-planting policy
mix_items.summary: Subsidies for emerging technology that allows seafood to be produced on land would boost the UK's food security and deliver significant climate benefits, new research shows.

mix_items.title: Q&A: Discovery could lead to a cure for glaucoma with nanotherapy
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Virginia and Northwestern University have created a tool that could help cure glaucoma.

mix_items.title: Removing cGAS protein may make aging worse by unleashing inflammatory DNA
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Rochester thought that shutting down a protein linked to inflammation might help slow aging. Instead, they found the opposite: Without the protein, mice became frailer, experienced more inflammation and had shorter life spans.

mix_items.title: How we manage and engage with horses may shape their personality
mix_items.summary: A new study reveals that horse personality is not only a matter of genetics, age or breed but also systematically linked to how horses are housed, ridden and cared for, and to the quality of the relationship they share with their owners. The findings underscore the importance of everyday management decisions for equine personality and welfare.

mix_items.title: Anemia in pregnancy linked to differences in babies' brain development
mix_items.summary: Researchers using a portable MRI scanner found that measurable differences in brain volumes emerged at around 12 months of age, offering some of the earliest evidence yet that maternal anemia shapes infant brain development in the first year of life and beyond.

mix_items.title: Women with cerebral palsy miss vital gynecologic care, study finds
mix_items.summary: As more individuals with cerebral palsy live well into adulthood, medical professionals are taking a closer look at the unique long-term health care needs of this patient population. While adults with cerebral palsy require the same routine health maintenance as anyone else, a large national study conducted at Yale showed that women living with cerebral palsy received significantly less preventive gynecologic care than women without the condition.

mix_items.title: The Future We Choose: New Beyond Blue report explores the forces shaping the next decade of mental health in Australia
mix_items.summary: Beyond Blue has launched "The Future We Choose: Mental health support in Australia through the next decade of change," a new strategic foresight report by Australia's national science agency, CSIRO, exploring how mental health in Australia may evolve over the next decade and the choices that could help shape a stronger, more connected and resilient future.

mix_items.title: New AI model for DNA learns from evolution to unlock secrets of the human genome
mix_items.summary: More than two decades after scientists first sequenced the entire human genome—all 3 billion base pairs, of DNA code—the meaning of much of this code remains a mystery.

mix_items.title: Petrochemical industry emissions could climb 50% by 2050, global mapping suggests
mix_items.summary: Carbon emissions from the petrochemical industry could increase by 50% by 2050, according to new research from the University of Sheffield. The study, published in Nature Sustainability, provides the most detailed data to date on emissions from one of the world's biggest emitters of carbon dioxide.

mix_items.title: White is more than a color: How nature inspired a new sustainable way to make white, water-repellent materials
mix_items.summary: Look closely at Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa, one of Japan's most iconic masterpieces. The brilliant white of the waves, snow on Mount Fuji and clouds above contain no white pigment. Instead, their whiteness comes from the way light scatters off the unprinted fibers of the washi paper itself.

mix_items.title: First Denisovan forearm bone discovered in southwest China
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered various Denisovan remains in Southwest China dating to the late Middle Pleistocene, including the first Denisovan radius—one of two long bones in the forearm.

mix_items.title: Improved health should guide obesity treatment, not weight loss alone
mix_items.summary: A new scientific statement released today by the Endocrine Society highlights the benefits of obesity treatment beyond weight loss, including improved overall health and reduced risk of conditions such as heart disease, sleep apnea and liver disease.

mix_items.title: A 'wholistic' view of cellular communication across an entire animal
mix_items.summary: It can't be heard, but different parts of the human body are in constant conversation, communicating to keep the entire system running efficiently. For biologists, being able to listen in on this discussion is a long-sought-after goal. Over the years, researchers have caught snippets of these exchanges, but the complete dialogue has remained out of reach.

mix_items.title: Clinical trial supports adding mental health care to routine preparation for major surgery
mix_items.summary: Facing major surgery is stressful, but for older adults, unaddressed anxiety and depression can impede physical recovery. A clinical trial led by researchers at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis found that starting an intervention before surgery—one that combines mental health coaching with optimization of medications that may increase risks for older adults—reduces postsurgery anxiety and depression.

mix_items.title: Marine conservation collides with mining in Indonesia’s biodiversity-rich Moramo Bay
mix_items.summary: SOUTH KONAWE, Indonesia — A marine protected area in Indonesia’s Southeast Sulawesi province is home to a critically depleted population of humphead wrasse. The species presence helped the area gain its protected status, but mining permits overlap parts of the conservation zone and line its coast. A 2024 government survey, published the following year, found […]

mix_items.title: Stanford scientists discover a seafood that can reverse signs of aging
mix_items.summary: A substance found in edible sea squirts appeared to reverse several signs of aging in older mice. Plasmalogen supplements improved memory and learning, strengthened connections between brain cells, reduced inflammation, and even helped the mice grow thicker, darker hair. Researchers believe the compounds may encourage brain regeneration and protect aging synapses.

mix_items.title: Scientists reveal the hidden instructions that build the human brain
mix_items.summary: UCLA researchers have discovered two powerful influences that help guide how the human brain forms before birth. Radial glia, stem cells responsible for producing much of the cerebral cortex, change their behavior depending on how they process glucose and on physical contact with signals arriving from the thalamus. Those signals can alter which types of neurons are produced, including upper-layer neurons that are especially prominent in humans.

mix_items.title: New injectable treatment helps the brain rebuild after stroke
mix_items.summary: Duke researchers developed an injectable scaffold that helped stroke-damaged brains grow new blood vessels, support nerve regrowth, and recover movement in mice. The treatment appears to work partly by recruiting the body’s own immune cells, including neutrophils that may switch from damaging to helpful under the right conditions.

mix_items.title: Galaxy Gallery: Galactic Gems Glisten in New Gallery From NASA’s Chandra
mix_items.summary: This gallery displays a collection of 16 galactic images from Chandra and other telescopes. Astronomers put galaxies into three main categories: spirals like our own Milky Way, ellipticals that are older and likely the results of mergers, and irregulars that can encompass a wide range of galactic phenomena. All types are represented in this collection. Each galactic image contains X-ray data from Chandra combined with data from telescopes such as NASA’s Webb, Hubble, IXPE, Swift, and NuSTAR, and others both in space and on the ground. mix_items.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
mix_items.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

mix_items.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

mix_items.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
mix_items.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

mix_items.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
mix_items.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.
